initialize.instructions:
Hindcast lets an agent check infrastructure decisions before they ship.

REAL SYSTEMS (production telemetry): connect_telemetry (Prometheus URL, plus Jaeger or Tempo for traces, optionally the cloud bill) → collect_telemetry (history into the workspace) → calibrate_model (read its trust report) → suggest_changes for "what should we change / where can we save", and verify_change for any change you propose or are asked about: a strategy, a Kubernetes manifest diff, a Terraform plan, or edited manifests against read_cluster's snapshot. Start a session with model_status: the workspace (./.hindcast) may already hold a fresh model.
Report verify_change results with their verdict AND confidence. "pass" with confidence "low" means the change pushes a service past anything the history showed: say so and recommend a load test instead of calling it safe. Quote the money as a range when the band is wide, and say when prices are list prices rather than the bill. Never present a backtest as a guarantee.
Everything is read-only towards the user's systems; nothing is applied. Credentials are passed as env var names, never as values.

DESIGNS ON PAPER: verify_design checks a spec you wrote (failures, headroom, cost vs budget) and returns fixes as exact spec changes; apply them and verify again until it passes.

ENGINE DETAILS: Hindcast simulates distributed-system architectures under load and failure.
Two engines: "fluid" (queueing model, milliseconds, used for quick checks and search) and "des" (discrete-event, every request simulated: real p50/p99/p99.9, emergent retry storms/timeouts/breakers, seeded). Use analyze for Monte Carlo confidence intervals and optimize_cost for the cheapest sizing that meets an SLO.
Describe a system as an architecture spec: components (id, kind, optional knobs) + connections ([caller, callee]) + optional zones (failure domains).
Kinds: client (traffic source), cdn, lb, gateway, server, worker, function, cache, db, replica, storage, queue, llm (self-hosted GPU), llmapi (hosted model API), external (someone else's service: its rate limit and latency, not its capacity), kv (managed NoSQL on demand: billed per request, a hot key throttles at one partition), dns (health-checked answers; failover lags by the health check and the TTL).
Rules: instances are only reachable behind lb/gateway/queue; db shares reads with replica children and fails over to them, and splits its keys over `shards` (a hot key still lands on one); cache/cdn need an origin behind them.
Dynamics: server/worker/llm can autoscale ({ min, max, targetUtil, warmupS, cooldownS }); caches go cold after a restart or flush-cache and re-warm over warmupS (thundering herd on the origin); a connection can carry network latency ({ from, to, latencyMs }).
Scenarios: duration, constant rps or traffic keyframes, readRatio, timed events (kill-id, kill, fail-zone, degrade, inject-errors, inject-latency, flush-cache, restore…), SLO.
For "is this design production-ready / what breaks first / what should we fix", call audit_resilience: it replays every failure mode, grades user impact, and returns verified fixes priced in $/month.
Calibrate to a real system by overriding capacity (req/s per instance), latencyMs and costPerHour per component.
Results are directional: good for comparing designs and finding bottlenecks, not a substitute for load tests.
For real systems with recorded telemetry, use backtest_strategy (replays production history through a calibrated model, with measured accuracy) and replay_outage (famous public outages against that model).

tools.name: list_components
tools.title: List component types
tools.description: Component kinds with default capacity, latency, price and knobs, plus size tiers and language runtimes. Call this before writing a spec.

tools.name: validate_architecture
tools.title: Validate an architecture spec
tools.description: Schema check plus architectural lint (unreachable instances, caches without origin, dangling connections…).

pricing.description: cost model: illustrative teaching defaults, or cited AWS us-east-1 / Google Cloud us-central1 on-demand prices

id.description: Unique id, also used as the display name unless `name` is set

kind.description: Component type — see list_components for capacities, latency and price

tier.description: Vertical size: S ×1, M ×2, L ×4 capacity

instances.description: server/worker/llm: horizontal instances (reachable only behind lb/gateway/queue)

limit.description: gateway/llmapi/external/kv rate limit or function max concurrency, req/s

timeoutMs.description: client deadline; slower responses count as failures

fallback.description: serve a degraded response while the breaker is open

routing.description: split evenly (default), call all children in parallel, or fail over in order

stallRate.description: share of requests that hit a rare stall (GC pause, compaction, noisy neighbour)

fanout.description: each call goes to N partitions of the callee in parallel; the caller waits for the slowest (scatter-gather)

queueS.description: bounded queue length in seconds of work

autoscale.description: server/worker/llm: target-tracking autoscaling; `instances` is the starting size

warmupS.description: launch → serving, seconds (default 30; EC2 ASG 90–180, k8s pod 5–20)

cooldownS.description: wait after scaling before scaling in (default 60)

warmupS.description: cache/cdn: re-warm time constant after a restart or flush (default 20 s)

writePolicy.description: cache/cdn: writes go on to the origin (through, default), or are acknowledged at the cache and flushed ~5 s later — fast, but lost if the cache dies first (behind)

workingSetGb.description: cache: the data it fronts, GB — with it the hit rate follows from the cache size (S 6.4, M 13, L 26 GB) and `skew`

skew.description: cache: how concentrated reads are on popular keys (Zipf exponent, default 1)

shards.description: db/replica: horizontal partitions, each a full database of its own — capacity and cost × shards; keys are spread by hash (give a sharded database's replica the same count)

hotKeyShare.description: db/kv: share of its traffic on one key (a celebrity, a hot counter): it all lands on one shard, which saturates first

ttlS.description: dns: how long clients cache an answer, s (default 60) — a dead target keeps getting traffic until it expires

healthCheckS.description: dns: how long health checks take to notice a dead target, s (default 30; 3 checks × 10 s)

latencyMs.description: network round trip added to every call over this link (cross-AZ ≈ 1, cross-region ≈ 60–150)

calls.description: calls per request over this link, made in parallel; the caller needs every one (a tweet written to N timelines, N lookups per page)

carries.description: the link takes only reads or only writes (CQRS: reads to a cache or replica, writes to a queue); default both

replication.description: database → replica: sync — every write waits for this replica (no data lost on failover, writes stop while it is unreachable); async (default) — the replica lags, a failover loses what it had not received

connections.description: caller → callee pairs, e.g. "lb -> api", ["lb","api"] or { from, to, latencyMs }; order matters for failover routing

members.description: component ids located in this failure domain

tools.name: simulate
tools.title: Simulate an architecture
tools.description: Run one scenario (traffic shape + failure events) against an architecture. Returns SLO compliance, error rate, p99, cost, ranked bottlenecks with plain-English explanations, and an event log. Set include_timeline for a per-second series.

tools.name: compare_architectures
tools.title: Compare architecture variants
tools.description: Test hypotheses: run a baseline plus variants (full specs or edit lists: set / add / remove / connect / disconnect) under the same scenario. Returns variants ranked — SLO-compliant first, then by cost — with each one's top bottleneck.

tools.name: analyze
tools.title: Monte Carlo analysis (discrete-event)
tools.description: Run the discrete-event engine N times with different seeds (in parallel) and report means with 95% confidence intervals for error rate, p50/p99/p99.9 and cost, the probability the SLO is met, and which component is the bottleneck how often. Use this before making a claim about a design.

tools.name: optimize_cost
tools.title: Find the cheapest configuration that meets the SLO
tools.description: Sizes the existing topology (instances, tiers, optionally language runtimes) to the cheapest configuration that meets the SLO under the scenario — growing under-provisioned components and shrinking over-provisioned ones — then verifies with discrete-event Monte Carlo. Returns before/after cost, monthly savings and the exact changes (as a variant you can pass to compare_architectures or open_in_app). Include failure events in the scenario if the result must survive them (e.g. N+1).

tools.name: audit_resilience
tools.title: Failure audit: what breaks first, and what it costs
tools.description: Replays one minute at the expected load once per production failure mode — every component dying (one instance or all), every zone going dark, each dependency turning slow (+250 ms) or erroring (20 %), caches restarting cold, a 3× traffic surge — plus the breaking point. Grades each incident by user impact (critical / major / minor / ok), detects self-healing and metastable non-recovery, lists the blast radius, and proposes fixes that are verified by re-running the same incident and priced in $/month. Returns a resilience score, the availability its structure promises (components in sequence multiply, redundant ones back each other up: nines, downtime a year, the weakest links) and a ranked risk register, plus a Markdown report. Ask the user for their expected req/s and what a minute of outage costs them.

tools.name: import_terraform
tools.title: Import an architecture from Terraform
tools.description: Convert `terraform show -json` output (state or saved plan) into an architecture spec priced with AWS us-east-1 SKUs. Resolves real wiring (CloudFront origins, ALB listeners → target groups → ASG/ECS/instances, API Gateway integrations, Lambda event sources, RDS replicas) and reports every heuristic it had to use (cache-aside reads, queue producers, hit rates) in `assumptions` — confirm those with the user, then simulate/optimize. Ask the user for request rates and SLOs; Terraform has neither.

tools.name: import_kubernetes
tools.title: Import an architecture from Kubernetes manifests
tools.description: Convert Kubernetes manifests (kubectl -o yaml, Helm template output, kustomize build — one or many YAML documents) into an architecture spec. Deployments/StatefulSets become components (images identify databases, caches, brokers, inference servers); HPAs become autoscaling; Ingress / LoadBalancer Services become entry points; call edges are inferred from Service names referenced in env vars and args. Every guess is listed in `assumptions` — confirm them with the user, ask for request rates and SLOs, then simulate or audit.

manifests_yaml.description: the manifests as YAML text (multi-document allowed)

tools.name: open_in_app
tools.title: Open in the Hindcast app
tools.description: Return a link that opens the architecture in the visual app (sandbox), or — with `compare_with` — side by side with a variant in Compare mode, optionally running a scenario. Use it to turn an analysis into a live demo. The app must be running (npm run dev).

warmupS.description: launch → serving, seconds (default 30; EC2 ASG 90–180, k8s pod 5–20)

cooldownS.description: wait after scaling before scaling in (default 60)

warmupS.description: cache/cdn: re-warm time constant after a restart or flush (default 20 s)

writePolicy.description: cache/cdn: writes go on to the origin (through, default), or are acknowledged at the cache and flushed ~5 s later — fast, but lost if the cache dies first (behind)

workingSetGb.description: cache: the data it fronts, GB — with it the hit rate follows from the cache size (S 6.4, M 13, L 26 GB) and `skew`

skew.description: cache: how concentrated reads are on popular keys (Zipf exponent, default 1)

shards.description: db/replica: horizontal partitions, each a full database of its own — capacity and cost × shards; keys are spread by hash (give a sharded database's replica the same count)

hotKeyShare.description: db/kv: share of its traffic on one key (a celebrity, a hot counter): it all lands on one shard, which saturates first

ttlS.description: dns: how long clients cache an answer, s (default 60) — a dead target keeps getting traffic until it expires

healthCheckS.description: dns: how long health checks take to notice a dead target, s (default 30; 3 checks × 10 s)

zone.description: place it in this zone (failure domain)

oneOf.description: add a link, or with link properties set them on an existing one
database: this share of its traffic goes to one key — a celebrity, a hot counter — all on one shard (0 ends it)
cut every link between two zones; both keep running

tools.name: backtest_strategy
tools.title: Backtest infrastructure changes on recorded production history
tools.description: Replay real traffic through a calibrated model (hindcast calibrate → model.json, hindcast import → dataset.json) with each strategy applied: $ saved/spent per month, minutes out of SLO, failed requests, worst moment and why, with 10th–90th percentile bands, ranked. Strategies are YAML/JSON objects: { name, changes: [{ service, replicas | autoscale | cpu | memoryGb | arch | perf | capacityRps | cache | readReplicas | zone | region } | { endpoint, retries, timeoutMs }] }. Reference models ship in reference/<system>/model.json and dataset.json.

model.description: path to model.json (default: the workspace model)

dataset.description: path to dataset.json (default: the workspace dataset)

last.description: only the last part of the history, e.g. "14d", "6h"

tools.name: replay_outage
tools.title: Would this design have survived a famous outage?
tools.description: Replay a public outage's published timeline against a calibrated model, as built and with strategies. Outages: cloudflare-2019-07-02 (Cloudflare, 2 July 2019 — a regex ate every CPU); github-2018-10-21 (GitHub, 21 October 2018 — 43 seconds, 24 hours); slack-2021-01-04 (Slack, 4 January 2021 — the Monday after the holidays); aws-use1-2025-10-20 (AWS us-east-1, 20 October 2025 — DynamoDB lost its DNS).

model.description: path to model.json (default: the workspace model)

rps.description: your normal load (default: p90 of the model history)

tools.name: connect_telemetry
tools.title: Connect to telemetry (Prometheus, Jaeger/Tempo, bill)
tools.description: Point Hindcast at the system's live telemetry and probe it, read-only: which metric presets Prometheus supports, which services it names, how far back data goes; which services Jaeger or Tempo knows and which ones requests enter through. Saves the connection in the workspace (credentials only as env var names). Call this first; calling it again merges new settings. Returns problems to fix and what the model will be able to know.

selector.description: label matchers added to every query, e.g. cluster="prod-eu"

namespaces.description: Kubernetes namespaces the system runs in (default: the namespaces holding the traced services)

presets.description: default: every preset whose metrics exist

tokenEnv.description: env var holding a bearer token (the token itself never goes in the workspace)

url.description: Jaeger query UI/API base, e.g. http://jaeger:16686

tokenEnv.description: env var holding a bearer token (the token itself never goes in the workspace)

url.description: Tempo HTTP API base, e.g. http://tempo:3200

tokenEnv.description: env var holding a bearer token (the token itself never goes in the workspace)

traceFiles.description: OTLP JSON lines or Jaeger JSON files (globs ok), instead of a trace backend

cur.description: AWS Cost and Usage Report CSV

tag.description: cost-allocation tag naming the component, e.g. user:service

timeoutMs.description: client deadline: slower answers count as failures

rename.description: raw service names → one id across sources

hostedBy.description: in-process dependencies seen in traces → the service they run in

entry.description: services requests enter through (default: found in traces)

ignore.description: services outside the system, e.g. load generators (default: client-only services in traces)

exclude.description: services to drop from the collected history: another system sharing the Prometheus (collect_telemetry lists services no trace touches)

tools.name: collect_telemetry
tools.title: Collect history from the connected telemetry
tools.description: Query Prometheus over a window, fetch traces spread across it from Jaeger/Tempo, add the bill, and import everything into the workspace dataset. Reports per service which signals exist (request rate, errors, p99, CPU, CPU limit, replicas, traces) and what is missing. Longer history with a busy peak makes a better model: one overload in the history is worth more than a month of quiet days.

last.description: how much history, e.g. "6h", "7d", "14d" (default 24h, or what the data covers)

start.description: window start (ISO or epoch s), instead of last

end.description: window end (default now, or the newest data)

stepS.description: bucket size in seconds (default: window / ~1000, at least 30)

maxTraces.description: traces to fetch, spread over the window (default 3000)

windows.description: several windows instead of one — an ordinary week plus a load test, say. A calm history never shows where latency turns; one load test in it teaches the model

tools.name: calibrate_model
tools.title: Calibrate a model of the system from the collected history
tools.description: Fit the model: capacity per replica (with its band) and what limits it (CPU, a lock or pool), latency, errors and cost per service; endpoint paths from traces. Holds back the last part of the history to measure accuracy on data the model never saw. Returns a trust report: services whose limit the history actually reached, services whose capacity is extrapolated, and services the model cannot explain. Read it before relying on verify_change.

holdout.description: share of the history held back to measure accuracy (default 0.3; 0 to skip)

listPrices.description: price services without a bill line at AWS Fargate list prices (default true)

tools.name: model_status
tools.title: What the workspace holds
tools.description: Connections, the collected history (window, age), the model (fit and trust per service, accuracy), recent reports, warnings (stale history, unmeasured accuracy) and the next step. Cheap: call it at the start of a session to see what is already there.

tools.name: verify_change
tools.title: Verify an infrastructure change against real history
tools.description: Backtest one or more changes over the collected history, before they ship: $ per month saved or spent (with its 10–90% band), minutes out of SLO added or removed, failed requests, the worst moment and why, endpoints that get worse, headroom before and after. A change is a strategy (object or YAML), a Kubernetes manifest diff (base/head), a Terraform plan (`terraform show -json`), or edited manifests against the live cluster snapshot from read_cluster. Each result has verdict pass | fail | inconclusive and a confidence (high | medium | low) that says which services the change pushes past anything the history showed. Writes an HTML and Markdown report for a human.

strategy.description: a strategy object or YAML: { name, changes: [{ service, replicas | autoscale | cpu | memoryGb | cpuRequest | memoryRequestGb | arch | perf | capacityRps | cache | readReplicas | zone | region } | { endpoint, retries, timeoutMs }] }

base.description: manifests before: a directory, a file, or YAML text

terraformPlan.description: path to `terraform show -json plan.out` output, or the JSON itself

head.description: the edited manifests (directory, file or YAML text)

last.description: only the last part of the history, e.g. "7d"

gateMinutes.description: minutes out of SLO a change may add before it fails (default 0.5)

window.description: replay only this part of the history — the ordinary week, when the history also holds a load test (the model still learned from all of it)

traffic.description: replay the history at another load — scale ×N, or peakRps for its busiest moment — to ask "does it survive launch day / Black Friday?"; the as-built system sees the same load

tools.name: suggest_changes
tools.title: What should we change? Fixes and savings, backtested
tools.description: Generates candidate changes from the history itself and backtests them all: services that ran out of capacity get fixes (more replicas — of the host for an in-process dependency —, more CPU or CPU autoscaling when CPU-bound); services that idled get savings (fewer replicas, smaller CPU, Graviton). Returns the fixes that cut minutes out of SLO and the savings that pass, cheapest first, each with its verdict and confidence, the passing savings tried together, and what was rejected. Use it for "what should we change?", "where can we save?" or after a fail, then verify_change the one to ship.

idleBelow.description: a service is idle below this share of capacity at its busiest (default 0.35)

tools.name: find_headroom
tools.title: How much more traffic the system can take
tools.description: The req/s the calibrated model sustains within SLO with today's endpoint mix, and which service saturates first — as built, and optionally with a strategy applied.

tools.name: review_capacity
tools.title: Capacity review: headroom, busier days, node loss, binding limits, fixes and savings
tools.description: The capacity review a platform team does by hand, from the calibrated history, every number backtested: headroom over the busiest moment and what saturates first; whether 1.5× and 2× today's traffic hold; what losing a node at the peak costs and the single points of failure (Kubernetes), with the replicas that fix it; services held back by CPU quota throttling or near their memory limit; and the fixes and savings that pass. Writes a Markdown report into the workspace. Use it for "how are we doing?", "weekly capacity review", "are we ready for next week?".

tools.name: check_node_loss
tools.title: Does it survive losing a Kubernetes node at its busiest?
tools.description: Replays the history's busiest moment with each node gone: every pod on it disappears at once (from kube_pod_info placement at the end of the history), services left with no replica are down, the rest serve on what is left, and Kubernetes brings the pods back after NotReady plus the default 300 s eviction toleration and a start (or never, when a fixed node pool has no room). Returns per node what it takes down, the minutes out of SLO and failed requests it adds, and the services one node failure takes out entirely. With a strategy, its replica changes are spread evenly over the nodes. Use it for "can we lose a node?", "is 2 replicas enough?", "where are our single points of failure?".

strategy.description: check under this strategy instead of as built

zones.description: lose a whole availability zone (every node in it) instead of one node — zones come from the nodes' provider ids (AWS, GCP)

tools.name: verify_design
tools.title: Verify a system design (no history needed)
tools.description: Check an architecture spec an agent wrote or proposes: validate it, simulate it at the expected load, replay every failure (instance and component deaths, zone loss, slow and erroring dependencies, cold caches, a 3× surge), measure headroom and cost against a budget. Verdict pass | pass with risks | fail, with findings and verified fixes that list the exact spec changes to apply. Use list_components to write the spec. Numbers come from catalogue defaults unless the spec overrides capacity, latency and cost.

rps.description: expected load (default: half the breaking point)

budgetMonthly.description: $ per month the design must fit in

incidentCostPerMinute.description: what a minute of outage costs, to price risk

tools.name: read_cluster
tools.title: Snapshot a Kubernetes cluster's workloads (read-only)
tools.description: Run `kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,hpa -o json` against an explicitly named context and save the snapshot: replicas, CPU and memory limits, autoscalers and architecture per workload. Never uses the current context implicitly and never runs anything but get. Then verify_change with { cluster: { head } } backtests edited manifests against what is running.

context.description: kube context name — required, never implied

prompts.name: verify-infra-change
prompts.title: Verify an infrastructure change on real history
prompts.description: Backtest a proposed change (strategy, manifests, Terraform plan) and report a verdict with its confidence

arguments.name: change
arguments.description: the change, in words, or a path to manifests / a plan

prompts.name: check-my-design
prompts.title: Check a system design
prompts.description: Write the design as a spec, find what breaks first, and fix it until it passes

resources.name: Hindcast live canvas
resources.description: The Hindcast simulator, rendering a spec or comparison live
